The Story of Shakatal Muni

I bow to the feet of Lord Jinendra, who bestows happiness and brings welfare to the world, and I write the story of Shakatal Muni.

King Nand of Pataliputra (Patna) had two ministers — Shakatal and Vararuchi. Shakatal was a Jain, and therefore had unwavering faith in Jain dharma. Vararuchi was not a Jain, and therefore hated Jain dharma and those who practised it. He was full of envy. Thus Shakatal and Vararuchi could never get along — they were completely opposed to each other.

One day, the great Jain scholar Mahapadya Muni came to Patna with his monastic group. Shakatal went to see him. With great devotion, he worshipped him and sat to hear the sacred discourse on lay and monastic dharma. The discourse had a profound effect on Shakatal's religious and tender heart. At that very moment, he broke all the nets of worldly delusion and took initiation, becoming a monk. Afterward, he thoroughly studied the doctrinal scriptures under his guru. Within a few days, Shakatal Muni attained great proficiency in several subjects. The guru, seeing his intelligence, scholarship, power of argument, and above all his natural talent, was very pleased. He gave him the position of Acharya.

From there, Shakatal Muni travelled through many lands, cities, and villages, teaching dharma and spreading the Jain faith. He guided many onto the pure path of self-welfare and spread the light of Jain dharma everywhere, a dharma that destroys the sufferings of lower births. While thus propagating dharma, he came to Patna once again.

One day, Shakatal Muni was having alms in the king's inner quarters and was heading toward the meditation grove. Minister Vararuchi saw him. This sinner, seeing a good opportunity to take revenge for an old grudge, said to Nand, "Maharaj, do you know that your old minister, the sinful Shakatal, has entered the inner quarters, the women's quarters, under the pretext of begging and has done some mischief! I received the news after he left, otherwise I would have had him arrested long ago and punished for his crime. Therefore, it is not proper for you to sit quietly for such tricksters." Truly, sinful people destined for lower births do not fail to commit the worst of sins.

Nand, led astray by his minister's words, became furious. He ordered his guards to arrest Shakatal Muni. But the monk, through his spiritual power, remained unmoved. He continued his walk peacefully, ignoring the threats. The guards, seeing his divine calm, could not bring themselves to harm him. They returned and told the king what they had seen. Nand's anger subsided, and he realised the folly of listening to Vararuchi's malicious words.

Shakatal Muni continued his spiritual practice and ultimately attained liberation. Vararuchi, through his hatred and false accusations, fell into lower births and suffered greatly.

This story teaches that the wicked will always try to harm the righteous, but the righteous, through their spiritual power and equanimity, remain unharmed. The wise should cultivate inner peace and not be provoked by the malicious words of others.
